title: Show HN: AJX – Find out where AI agents get stuck using your product
summary: Hi HN. I made AJX (Agent Journey Experience). It is a CLI and skill bundle that you run to test what your product feels like to use from the point of view of an agent, and you get back a list of "asks" that would improve your product from an agentic usability perspective: so that agents spend less time, tokens and retries to accomplish tasks with it. How? It works by having an outer loop (AJX harness skill + CLI) that controls an "inner loop": the agent that actually tries out your product. The outer loop investigates the inner loop once it finishes. To try it, copy the prompt from the main page into your favorite agent and it will install the skill and CLI and you can then trigger /ajx skill, give it a prompt and some simple configuration as text, and it helps you with the rest. The outer loop starts loading the configured harness of your choice (claude, codex, kiro-cli etc..) in an environment and configuration of your choice (docker, VM, local, with or without specific skills, specific model, amount of runs, and more), and provides the harness (inner loop) with your input prompt and links, and "definition of done" - what does it mean to succeed with this product? For example with vercel cli you could say "build and deploy a simple hello world with vercel CLI [link]" as the prompt for the AJX test. Once the inner loop harness runs its course, the outer harness loop examines the run, logs and details, and outputs and extract the needed information from that run: retries, tokens, mistakes, assumptions and more, and created a very detailed report, as well as a list of asks that if applied to the product, would improve the agentic journey given the same prompt in the future. I call this "Agent Journey eXperience" it's the agentic equivalent of "User Experience" - if we were to document the journey an agent does when trying your product for the first time in a specific scenario. - Where does it go astray and makes mistakes? - How many retries does it take to succeed with the task? - How much time? - How many tokens? List of ASKS as an output: What features/fixes would the agent want the product to have to save it from making these mistakes or costing extra time and token in the future? here are some examples: - CLI missing a --JSON, which cost lots of parsing of unneeded code - CLI missing commands like doctor, help aliases - DOCS disagree with behavior of the product - Skills pull the agent in the wrong direction - lack of feedback while product is executing - Human friendly CLIs outputs break the agent loop - and much more. Why? I'm a startups solutions architect @ AWS, and previously wrote the art of unit testing and did lots of work on code quality, engineering practiced and continuous delivery) I built AJX (ajx.dev) when I was tasked with giving feedback on an internal upcoming AWS product that is meant to be used by agents. The team wanted feedback from potential users, and I figured that agents are the new potential users. I figured that if I was a product owner, I'd love to know what it feels like to work with my product (CLI, SDK, Website, Docs etc), and that the harder the agents work to use my product, the less people would point their agent at it, or the less the agent would tend to recommend it. Also I think it's useful to have "brag points" that your product is "agent-friendly". I even tested AJX with AJX and it found great of issues with the CLI (for example ajx status was returning the wrong status sometimes, ajx init --task behaved differently than expected, and other cool stuff like that. I envision this being used as part of a CI/CD cycle with a loop until AJX returns "all green" and no ASKS. AJX is still very new - so probably lots of rough edges but in an agent first world, I think it's a step in the right direction: see the world from an agent's POV.

title: Show HN: I asked HN about AI agentic setups, here are 750 of the comments mapped
summary: A few days back I posted here asking about how people were using AI / doing agentic coding (see: https://news.ycombinator.com/item?id=50366117 ). Needless to say, I was overwhelmed by the response! The one challenge I found, however, was that the comments were almost impossible to parse: some users answered my questions in the format I provided, others answered in any order, but either way it was really hard to get a picture of who was using what from that thread alone. So, I spent last night building an interactive site out of people's answers. I used Claude to pull the tools, models and plans out of each comment, with every number linked back to the original comments it came from. The website covers subscriptions, models, harnesses, orchestration and agent platforms, what people liked and disliked about each tool, and some of the better stories from the thread. Take a look and let me know what you think! ----- The interactive website: https://scouttyg.github.io/hn-agentic-setups/ The code: https://github.com/scouttyg/hn-agentic-setups

title: Leeroy: Making AI agents play World of Warcraft
story_key: story|title:leeroy making ai agents play world of warcraft
content_excerpt: I’ve been using AI coding agents daily for my work as a software engineer. I typically give them well-defined tasks that take me less than an hour to complete manually. But I don’t think I truly understand these tools. How do they approach a task that takes hours to complete? How do they plan, recover from mistakes, collaborate with other agents? How could I even measure this? So I decided to build a benchmark. I was inspired by RuneBench , a benchmark that has AI coding agents play RuneScape by writing code against an SDK. I played a lot of World of Warcraft during the Burning Crusade and Wrath of the Lich King expansions, and when I saw RuneBench I knew I wanted to try this in WoW. World of Warcraft has a mature private server implementation (AzerothCore). It’s a game that I know well, and it has content that is explicitly designed to be completed by a group. A dungeon designed for 5 players is a benchmark task that someone else has carefully designed and balanced for you. And you can’t complete it solo. World of Warcraft is a real-time game. A fight can be won or lost in less than 5 seconds. But an LLM-based agent works in turns, and one turn can take anywhere from 2 to 60 seconds. So the agents can’t directly control their character. Instead they control a headless game client, and they write Lua scripts that are executed by the game client. The scripts play the game in real time while the agent is thinking. The client doesn’t have a screen either. It communicates directly with the game server using the network protocol of World of Warcraft. It converts the information sent by the server into structured data that the agent can work with. For example, that there is a kobold 25 yards behind your character (and 3 yards lower), that the kobold can currently see your character, and will attack it if it comes 3 yards closer. When the agent wants to move their character, it requests a path through a navmesh pathfinder, which takes into account the collision models of the world. (This pathfinder was the source by far of the most bugs in the project). The SDK exposes all the information that a human player can see, and all the actions a human player can take. But nothing else. There is no “pull nearest mob” function, no “don’t let the agents cast any crowd-control abilities until I say so” function, no “position healers behind melee tanks” function. title: The Blueprint: Orchestrating 5,000+ AI assets for a World Cup TV spot
summary:
Welcome back to The Blueprint, a regular feature where we highlight how Google Cloud customers are tackling unique and common challenges across industries using the latest AI and cloud technologies. We hope to inspire others looking to innovate in their work.

AI is rapidly transforming video production at virtually every step of the process, from ideation and storyboarding to filming, editing, and release. At Mito, we’re striving to democratize AI-powered video creation, enabling everyone from solo artists to large enterprises to get the most out of the best creative technologies available.

The Challenge

When we founded Mito, our goal was to eliminate the complex technical friction that stops creators from telling long-form, narrative stories with generative AI. 

However, transitioning from a single five-second clip to a cohesive campaign — such as a 120-second national TV spot for Movistar Plus+, a part of Telefónica, to broadcast across Spain during the World Cup this summer. This effort revealed massive infrastructure and workflow bottlenecks:

  • Asset & workflow overhead: Managing local media libraries across individual workstations was unscalable. For Movistar alone, our production required generating a massive "iceberg" of over 5000 assets (1000 of those videos) generated in around 65 iteration rounds.

  • Zero real-time collaboration: Traditional feedback loops required manual downloads, Google Drive uploads, and fragmented communication across chat apps and email.

  • Rendering latency: Standard AI video rendering takes four to five minutes per short clip. Running these processes synchronously froze our user interface and stalled creative velocity.

  • Model disparity & consistency: Every generative model requires distinct prompting logic. Maintaining character persistence, specific lighting, and camera angles across dozens of shots — while preserving the likeness of real public figures like chef Ferran Adrià or journalist Juanma Castaño — was nearly impossible without central orchestration.

  • Capacity constraints: Operating on public pay-as-you-go model APIs left us vulnerable to rate limits and regional throughput throttling during peak traffic.

The Solution

To deliver an infinite, real-time creative canvas for filmmakers, we designed a serverless, asynchronous architecture built on Google Cloud.

We run our API, AI Director, and background workers as Java services on Cloud Run, which scales with request volume.

In order to address message routing challenges, we decoupled job execution using Google Cloud Pub/Sub as our central event bus. Long-running video generations are offloaded to background Cloud Run workers, allowing creators to keep working uninterrupted on the UI canvas.

To minimize latency, media assets are stored in Google Cloud Storage and delivered via Cloud CDN. Expiring key signatures keep pre-release client assets strictly private. Keeping our storage alongside the models we call through Vertex AI reduces network transfer delays.

An isolated database architecture helps with the heavy business intelligence and analytics workloads while mitigating potential negative impacts on production performance through Cloud SQL and PostgreSQL. We rely heavily on foundational models like Omni, Veo and Nano Banana, which we access through Vertex AI alongside our custom system prompts.

Finally, our structured canvas frontend enforces a "Rule of 6" (limiting prompt variables across World, Camera, Light, Texture, Actions, and Character) and prioritizes still-frame generation before video rendering to maximize cost efficiency.

The Architecture

The Outcome

By pairing our creative orchestration platform with Google Cloud’s infrastructure, we successfully delivered a landmark national broadcast campaign that the production team describes as 95% AI-generated:

  • Prime-time scale: The 120-second Movistar campaign for the Spanish National Team  aired across every major television channel in Spain, with 1,441 assets live on a single shared Canvas near launch.

  • AI Director copilot: Our conversational agent translates natural language instructions into precise model parameters while maintaining context, lighting, and visual style across every scene.

  • Seamless collaboration: Distributed teams and brand clients can work on the same canvas in real time. Because new generations are saved as separate assets instead of overwriting earlier ones, stakeholders can duplicate projects to explore parallel creative ideas.

  • Continuous dogfooding: Through our internal studio, Mito Films, we put our tools to the test on high-stakes client projects — whether that's global television spots or keynotes for top robotics startups — ensuring direct feedback flows back into engineering.

  • Future-proof foundation: Our architecture is primed for rendering times to collapse from minutes to seconds, positioning Mito to handle upcoming world models, deeper memory states, and personalized content delivery.

The Details

Building an enterprise-grade platform for AI storytelling required solving several backend and creative challenges. This includes our creation of a virtual queuing system that mitigates third-party API rate limiting during usage spikes for smooth request concurrency, with bounded retries and a clear outcome for every job.

Because creative output cannot be fully validated with standard unit tests, we built an automated evaluation harness powered by Gemini. Acting as an independent judge, it evaluates AI Director outputs against original user intents across an automated test suite, which we run alongside standard tests for high-impact Director changes.

We knew early on that we would need multi-model intelligence routing. As such, we built the AI Director to dynamically coordinate tasks across multiple specialized models — including Sonnet, Gemini, and ElevenLabs for audio — treating the spatial canvas like a live code repository to infer adjacent contextual cues.

We also needed to embrace an “imperfect aesthetic” to arrive at a more authentic outcome. In our Movistar spot, the story follows Tommy, a 17-year-old student making an AI video project. At the climax, the AI misunderstands a prompt, making coach Luis de la Fuente say "In the same milkshake" while holding a drink. Tommy edits the prompt live to "In the same heartbeat," and the video recalibrates instantly. 

By incorporating surreal visual elements — like stadium stands built into Galician cliffs or a neighborhood bar covered in pitch grass — we showcased how generative AI can elevate human storytelling rather than obscure it.

title: The Iron(wood) Throne: Google's TPU Stakes Its Claim on Inference
summary: Viable Alternative of CUDA Moat, NVIDIA scared and working nights & weekends, Jensen’s Counter Submission, Kimi K3, Muse Spark Open, Qwen, GLM5.3, TorchTPU, vLLM, SGLang, llm-d, Ray
story_key: story|title:the iron wood throne google s tpu stakes its claim on inference
content_excerpt: In November 2025, we published a newsletter saying that Google is selling TPUs to external customers. Since then, we have been proven right over and over again with Oracle, OpenAI , Anthropic, and Meta all becoming customers of TPUs just as our Accelerator Model reported. Hardware demand is only half the story, as NVIDIA’s moat has historically been its software and large developer ecosystem. This is where TPU is also making headway, partnering with upstream maintainers across the entire ecosystem, including the Meta PyTorch team, vLLM (Inferact, RedHat), SGLang (RadixArk), llm-d, Ray, etc. This is not a surprise to folks that have read our September 2026 article laying out Google TPU’s externalization strategy . Back in our September article, we published the first third-party TPUv7 results on InferenceX on single-turn workloads, showing that in an apples-to-apples FP8 comparison on Qwen 3.5 397B, TPUv7 Ironwood) delivered up to 50% better performance per dollar than B200 and B300. We also reported that many Google TPU customers were asking for AgentX results, since long-context, multi-turn agentic serving is where inference spend is heading. Previously, Jensen went on the Dwarkesh Podcast and commented on the fact that no other chips were taking advantage of their opportunity to show performance on InferenceX. Six months later, and indeed Google is taking full advantage of this opportunity. Today we are releasing the first official long-context, multi-turn, realistic agentic inference benchmark results on TPUv7 across four models, showing that TPUv7 is either competitive on perf per dollar for external customers or delivers the best state-of-the-art result: Muse Spark Open SGLang AgentX (NVFP4 weights): Competitive TPU performance per dollar result even though the architecture was co-designed for GPUs. Submitted by OSS ecosystem developer, RadixArk (Makers of SGLang). GLM-5.2 vLLM AgentX (FP8): TPUv7 is the cheapest FP8 option, delivering 1.2x to 2.7x the tokens per dollar of B200, B300, and MI355X from 60 to 300 tok/s/user. NVIDIA NVFP4 still beats TPUv7 FP8, but with accuracy / quality loss. Qwen3.5 vLLM AgentX (FP8): With llm-d disaggregated serving, TPUv7 beats GB300 FP8 at every interactivity level and restores parity even against GB300 FP4 at higher quality / accuracy. Kimi K3 vLLM AgentX (MXFP4 weights): Competitive with GB300 NVL72 at launch; With TPUv7 delivering 1.15x to 2.5x the tokens per dollar of GB200, B200, B300, and MI355X. Submitted by

title: claude-code v2.1.319
summary:
What's changed

  • Changed auto mode with telemetry or feature flags off, including behind LLM gateways: calls the server can't check are asked about or denied, with no fallback to the built-in classifier; set CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=0 to keep using it (Bedrock, Vertex and Foundry are unchanged)
  • Changed auto mode behind an LLM gateway: CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 turns on the server-side check even with CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_EXPERIMENTAL_BETAS set; if managed settings set the latter, they must set the 1 too
  • Added support for MCP tasks in the terminal: when an MCP server runs a tool call as a task, Claude Code moves it to the background right away and tells Claude the result when it finishes
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_MCP_TASK_BACKGROUND environment variable to make Claude Code wait for an MCP task inside its tool call instead of moving it to the background right away
  • Added permissions.denyInsteadOfPrompting setting: a tool call that would wait on a permission prompt is denied and the turn continues, in terminal sessions, subagents and teammates
  • Added /claude-api latency-optimize to find where your Claude API code makes people wait and try faster settings against your eval
  • Added the CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_FEATURE_FLAGS environment variable, which stops feature-flag fetching without turning off telemetry; every flag then uses its built-in default
  • Added spend for today, this week and this month to /usage for developers behind a Claude apps gateway who have no spend limit, when the gateway runs this version or later
  • Added admin.pooled_conflict_rule and admin.pooled_priority_order to the Claude apps gateway, to set which pooled group budget pays first for a developer in several groups
  • Added an optional login_notice setting to the Claude apps gateway that shows an operator-defined message on the gateway's browser verification page and on Claude Code's sign-in screen
  • Added CLAUDE_GATEWAY_LOG_FORMAT=json to the Claude apps gateway: operational log lines become JSON with severity, time and message, for log collectors that read the level from a field
  • Added a Claude apps gateway boot warning for a case where another policy's availableModels also allows a custom model id that one policy lists by name
  • Added start-up warnings to the Claude apps gateway for policies with no desktopHome that rely on coworkTabEnabled: false or chatSessionRetentionDays, ahead of Claude Desktop's November 10 change
  • Added a warning when your claude.ai login ends and Claude Code continues on the sign-in from ant auth login, which bills usage to your Claude Console organization
  • Added a line at startup naming the Claude Console organization that is billed in a case where Claude Code uses the sign-in from ant auth login
  • Added an "Earlier in this session" row to /tasks that lists finished subagents, so you can reopen one and message it even after it leaves the list or you restart
  • Added a note to /loop confirmations in cloud sessions that a timer stops with its container, with an offer of a loop that survives
  • Fixed MCP servers on the older handshake failing to connect, or returning empty results, because Claude Code declared an extension that it only uses with newer servers
  • Fixed a long-running MCP tool call on a claude.ai connector sometimes never reporting its result after --resume
  • Fixed a session's diff failing to load on claude.ai and the mobile apps when the folder Claude Code runs in has a file or folder named HEAD
  • Fixed /diff showing "Diff unavailable" when a git repository has a file or folder named HEAD at its top level
  • Fixed the /diff pane opening blank in sessions where 64 or more turns edited files
  • Fixed slash commands typed after a leading space, tab or newline being sent to Claude as plain text instead of running
  • Fixed a request that kept failing with a 401 refreshing your login on every retry and causing 401s in your other sessions
  • Fixed /context sending its full visual grid to Claude on every later turn; Claude now reads only the table
  • Fixed claude -p exiting 0 in auto mode when its actions were refused because no safety check was available: text and JSON output now exit 1
  • Fixed a case where Claude Code listed every project file at start on Linux for projects on a network file system (NFS, SMB, Lustre and similar)
  • Fixed a case where auto mode was wrongly refused when a client sent a model change and a request for auto mode back to back
  • Fixed /status showing "Auto mode server: Enabled" when the server-side review isn't reaching the session, for example behind an LLM gateway that drops it
  • Fixed Claude-drafted feedback, surveys and /feedback continuing to appear after the server refused feedback for your organization
  • Fixed Claude drafting feedback on third-party gateways, where it can't be sent
  • Fixed auto mode refusing actions without saying why when permission rules or autoMode settings are very large: it now explains and, unless autoMode deny rules are set, asks you in the terminal
  • Fixed a case where Bash deny and ask rules missed commands written with quoted words
  • Fixed subagent hand-back reports showing an internal marker and provenance note when expanded outside verbose mode
  • Fixed claude -p --resume with a prompt losing a deferred tool call when its MCP server is missing: the run now exits 1, keeps the call and refuses later input
  • Fixed a case where text was dropped from informational messages sent to SDK clients
  • Fixed a case where Agent SDK hosts got a generic exit-code error instead of a failed run's own error message when the disk was full
  • Fixed CLAUDE_CODE_RESUME_INTERRUPTED_TURN re-running a turn that was interrupted in plan mode when the session resumes in another permission mode
  • Fixed edits to a settings file being ignored when made within a few seconds of Claude Code writing that file
  • Fixed a config file left at the legacy name hiding your setup with no warning: Claude Code now says on stderr when a home holds two config files, and which is in use
  • Fixed ~/.claude.json, settings and edited files ending up empty or cut off when the disk fills during a save in a read-only folder or to a bind-mounted file (one session saving at a time)
  • Fixed Write ending the turn as a refusal when it couldn't read the file to overwrite
  • Fixed background Bash commands that finish almost instantly losing their output while being reported as completed
  • Fixed the Bash tool's diff of changed files missing a file that the command wrote just before it ended
  • Fixed a mistyped model name, such as opus-5-5, telling you to update Claude Code instead of suggesting the model you meant
  • Fixed a case where NotebookEdit changed the wrong cell when the notebook changed while a permission prompt was open
  • Fixed a ~0.5s hang after pressing Enter on the /login success screen: the dialog now dismisses immediately and the post-login refresh runs in the background
  • Fixed Ctrl+G not opening the external editor while typing an "Other" answer to a question in screen reader mode
  • Fixed Monitor's WebSocket watch failing with "could not resolve" behind a proxy when CLAUDE_CODE_PROXY_RESOLVES_HOSTS is set and the machine has no DNS of its own
  • Fixed claude plugin eval warnings suggesting max: 0 for a tool that must not be called, which could never pass
  • Fixed background plugin auto-update not installing a dependency added by the updated plugin version
  • Fixed Cmd+click not opening links in Ghostty over tmux in sessions opened from the agents view
  • Fixed a mod's hot reload in .claude/skills missing a file that was deleted just after it appeared, and missing its return
  • Fixed /rewind failing with "No files were restored" when restoring code to a checkpoint from before /branch
  • Fixed the /claude-api skill saying Console web settings don't apply to Managed Agents sessions, and tightened its credential and permission examples
  • Fixed needless permission prompts for read-only commands wrapped in a plain timeout DURATION, such as timeout 30 rg foo
  • Fixed WebFetch describing claude.ai shared-chat links as empty pages; it now says shared chats can't be read and to paste the conversation instead
  • Fixed Artifact database calls being re-sent to artifacts without a database; errors now say whether republishing helps
  • Fixed a case where artifact database reads that save to a folder (out_dir) were refused
  • Fixed detailed beta tracing not presenting CLAUDE_CODE_CLIENT_CERT to collectors that require a client certificate
  • Fixed the OpenTelemetry claude_code.session.count metric counting Agent SDK prewarm() processes that were never claimed; a pre-started process now counts once, when it is claimed
  • Fixed /clear killing running commands of background agents, teammates and workflows that keep running, and foreground subagents of background agents and teammates
  • Fixed a terminal whose Claude apps gateway sign-in had expired sending telemetry and managed-settings requests that the gateway refused and logged as invalid_token
  • Fixed the agents view appearing to send a reply to a background session waiting on a permission prompt; the reply now stays in the box with a hint to open the session and answer
  • Fixed agent view removing a draft saved by another agent view in the same directory when exiting
  • Fixed a case where agent view came back with another agent view's input text after restarting itself for an update
  • Fixed the agents view preview cutting off long commands, results and status lines without an ellipsis, and dropping **, backticks and tags from commands waiting for approval
  • Fixed Claude in Chrome reporting the extension as not connected when the connection dropped mid-action; Claude now checks the page before repeating an action that may have run
  • Fixed Remote Control sessions still showing "Limit reached" on other devices after a usage limit was lifted outside the session
  • Fixed the file card sometimes missing in the Claude iOS app when Claude sent a single file
  • Fixed self-hosted runner sessions failing with no explanation when the server keeps refusing to renew model access: the runner now retries sooner and posts a warning in the session
  • Fixed /permissions in cloud sessions replying only that it isn't available; it now says where the session's rules live and how to change them
  • Fixed cloud sessions losing session-scoped deny and ask permission rules, such as those a PermissionRequest hook adds, when the session moves to a new worker
  • Fixed mod hot-reloading turning off for the session when you typed three messages instead of answering its question in a cloud session
  • Fixed background tasks that keep running after /clear disappearing from the task list in Claude Code on the web until another task started or ended
  • Fixed hidden commands appearing in the slash command menu of cloud sessions on mobile and web
  • Fixed a case where /rewind could restore or delete a file through a directory symlink
  • Fixed a case where a sed command could skip the permission check in accept-edits and auto mode
  • Fixed a case where CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_MODE_SERVER=1 in managed settings was ignored behind an LLM gateway when the gateway's URL is set only there and server-managed settings can't be fetched
  • Fixed a Bash permission bypass where a crafted environment prefix could hide part of a command from permission checks
  • Fixed a case where deny and ask rules, hook matchers and disallowedTools entries written with a claude.ai connector's terminal name (mcp__claude_ai_Slack) were ignored in Claude Desktop (takes effect once Claude Desktop includes this version)
  • Fixed a sandbox escape when creating a worktree
  • Fixed self-hosted runners: --trust-workspace false now also stops hooks in the repository's settings files and skills from running
  • Fixed a case where idle background sessions started through a shell-exported LLM gateway left the gateway after an update
  • Fixed help links in /status and the auto mode billing notice opening only part of the address when they wrap
  • Fixed a case where certificate errors behind a TLS-inspecting proxy persisted when CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_NONESSENTIAL_TRAFFIC was set. With it set, Claude Code now makes a TLS handshake with the configured API host after a certificate failure, through your http:// proxy if one is set; it sends no API request
  • Fixed claude remote-control exiting silently with status 0 when a first-run question gets no answer (scripts, services, batch jobs, Ctrl+C); it now says why and exits 1
  • Fixed claude remote-control ignoring a piped y that has no newline after it at the first-run question; it now counts as a yes
  • Fixed /rename reporting plain success when the new name could not be saved to the session transcript; it now warns that the new name may not last
  • Fixed ${CLAUDE_PLUGIN_ROOT} not being substituted in a plugin-provided subagentStatusLine command, which can now reference the plugin's own scripts
  • Fixed claude plugin update and /plugin "Update now" not installing dependencies added by the new plugin version
  • Fixed subagents being told after compaction to expect a completion notice for background agents they neither started nor took over
  • Fixed a case where a background agent's later report was lost silently: the notification now says it was refused and how to ask for it
  • Improved config saves on Windows: Claude Code waits longer for a file another program has open, so a kill during a save is less likely to leave ~/.claude.json empty
  • Improved Claude in Chrome after a brief disconnect: it waits up to 6 seconds for the session's own browser to return before picking another
  • Improved Claude in Chrome: javascript_tool results of up to 60,000 characters now stay in the conversation instead of being saved to a file
  • Improved claude purge and the clean-up of old sessions to retry a folder that could not be fully deleted, and to report it as an error if it remains
  • Improved the refusal for a path outside the working directories on macOS and Windows: when only its letter case differs from a path inside them, the message names that spelling
  • Improved the contrast of faint gray secondary text, such as hints, details in /stats, /model and /sandbox, and rejected-action messages
  • Improved the artifact database error when an update targets a document that does not exist, and when the service pauses repeated refused writes
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's warnings about a failed upstream call: each now names the upstream, not only its provider
  • Improved the Claude apps gateway's spend limit error: it reads "spend limit reached · resets Dec 1", then admin.blocked_message if one is set
  • Improved the /model picker: older models are now grouped under a "More models" row instead of being listed after the current ones
  • Improved /context at the terminal so the table Claude reads stays short: each list keeps its 10 largest rows, and MCP tools that load on demand share one row per server until they're called

title: Polarity Classification with Multitask Learning Syntax Augmentation
summary: Sentiment Analysis (SA) is a fundamental NLP task concerned with the identification and categorization of subjective information in text. While lexicon-based methods offer transparency, they often struggle with linguistic phenomena such as negation and intensification. Syntactic parsing has been integrated into SA pipelines to address this, but conventional parsers introduce significant computational overhead. Recent work shows that reformulating dependency parsing as a Sequence Labeling (SEL) task can improve efficiency. We propose and compare two strategies for integrating syntactic knowledge into a neural sentiment analysis model under unified Multi-Task Learning (MTL). The first, Standard-MTL, jointly learns dependency parsing (via sequence labeling) and sentiment polarity classification using a shared encoder with two task-specific heads. The second, Contrastive-MTL, provides implicit syntactic guidance through a contrastive auxiliary objective and a syntax-biased attention pooling mechanism, without requiring explicit label prediction. Both rely on syntactic annotations during training and eliminate need for hand-crafted compositional rules or external parsing at inference. We evaluate eleven datasets spanning seven languages---the MARC corpus (English, Spanish, French, German) and seven datasets from SemEval-2022 Task 10 (English, Spanish, Norwegian, Basque, Catalan)---using four established SEL encodings. With the relative encoding, Contrastive-MTL outperforms a syntax-naive baseline on 10 of 11 datasets and surpasses the external rule-based pipeline (SELSP) that parses at inference on all six datasets where the latter applies, while being 1.5--9$\times$ faster at evaluation. Standard-MTL is more dataset- and encoding-dependent. These results show implicit syntactic supervision during training can match or exceed explicit parsing at inference without computational overhead.

title: A Closer Look at Phonon TTS. Launching High-Quality On-Device Speech That Tops the Benchmarks.
story_key: story|variant:speech|title:a closer look at phonon tts launching high quality on device speech that tops th
content_excerpt: Two weeks ago, we opened up Phonon, our small text-to-speech model that runs on your own device. It needs no server and no network, and what you type stays with you. We've been very happy with the reception so far. So here's the story of the launch: why we built Phonon, what it can do, the demos that came with it, and how it did on Hugging Face's Open TTS Leaderboard. Most voice AI lives in the cloud: every sentence makes a round trip to a server. Phonon runs on your own device instead. Your text stays there and the voice works without a network. We’ve also opened the weights. Phonon 31m is Apache 2.0, so you can use it for free, even in a commercial product. The other models are CC BY-NC, so they’re free for non-commercial projects. If you’re building something commercial with those, pricing is based on your number of users, not how much speech you generate. Getting a good voice to run on a small device has always been hard. You could make the model small, but then it didn’t sound great. Or you could make it sound great, but then it wouldn’t fit. We addressed both. We announced Phonon in April and spent the next six months building on it with partners and early users. Their feedback helped us to shape this release. The models got smaller, and we added more languages and support for custom voices through voice cloning and voice design. Phonon is based on the Pocket TTS lineage and as such uses flow matching to generate the audio which is very different from the modeling techniques used in other TTS systems. This is what allowed us to bring this level of quality to such a small model but it created new challenges while training the models. The training was initially numerically unstable and required several tricks to produce quality results on all five languages. Phonon comes in two sizes, at about 65 MB and 75 MB. Together they speak English, French, German, Spanish and Portuguese. There are more than 100 built-in voices, and you can create your own in Gradium Studio . Phonon also handles the important things that most other TTS systems often stumble on, like phone numbers, dates and codes. It runs on phones, laptops, single-board computers and in a browser tab, so you can hear it right now . Phonon 31m speaks English and is Apache 2.0, so you can build on it freely, including for commercial products. Phonon 40m covers all five languages under a non-commercial license. title: Agents Are Going Async
summary: Async subagents let an agent stay responsive while background workers run long tasks. How the orchestrator, notifications and approvals work in Deep Agents.
content_excerpt: Imagine a chief of staff who disappears every time you hand them a big project and only comes back once it's done. You'd probably fire them immediately. A good chief of staff keeps projects moving in the background while staying reachable and keeping you updated along the way. As we ask agents to work toward bigger goals, they need the same two properties. An agent has to be responsive, acting on a new instruction right away with the context of everything before it, and productive, making progress on many large tasks at once. The architecture we've used to build agents for a while can't meet both requirements. In a standard ReAct loop, each long tool call blocks the loop and every other task queues behind it. Instead, we're seeing the ecosystem converge on a split between one agent that stays with the user and background workers that do the long work. Claude Code runs subagents in the background by default, OpenAI's dots hand work to background workers to make progress on several things at once, and DeepSeek Harness built its super agent around a router that talks to people and background workers that run tasks in parallel. We’re bringing this pattern to Deep Agents with async subagents . An orchestrator stays available to the user and keeps the conversation's context organized, while async subagents run as background workers and report back when they finish. The amount of work the agent can take on then grows with the number of background workers instead of the length of one loop. An agent runs in a loop. The model calls a tool, waits for the result, and decides what to do next. Historically, tools and subagents blocked that loop until they returned, like code that awaits each slow call in turn. An async subagent works like a task started with asyncio.create_task or a Promise you don't await yet. The call returns right away, the work runs independently in the background, and the result comes back later. Steering a running subagent is separate from reaching the orchestrator. When the orchestrator sends a follow-up with update_async_task , the update_strategy field on that subagent's definition decides what happens: Every unfinished task is listed in the orchestrator's system prompt, so it always knows what's in flight. It can poll with check_async_task or tasks can report back on their own : A subagent that needs approval shows up as waiting , and the user answers on the subagent's own thread without interrupting the orchestrator. title: Zero Mismatch, Simple Async RL: REINFORCE Zero, DeepSeek-V4.1 and Kimi K3.1
summary: Asynchronous RL trains on stale weights. Align rollout and training kernels bit for bit, and unclipped importance sampling corrects that lag. Plus zero-mismatch RL for DeepSeek-V4.1-Flash, Kimi K3.1 and AMD MI355X.
story_key: model:deepseek|ver:4.1|title:zero mismatch simple async rl reinforce zero deepseek v4 1 and kimi k3 1
content_excerpt: Last month, we showed that rollout and training can agree exactly. On DeepSeek-V4-Flash, vLLM and the trainer produced the same logprob for every sampled token, bit for bit, on the fast kernels, with an 8.7% reduction in rollout throughput. An agent skill now does the alignment for each new model. That post was about synchronous RL, which has no weight lag, so zero mismatch removes the only gap between rollout and training. This post is about asynchronous RL, which is faster but off-policy by design. Does zero mismatch still matter there? We answer with a new paper from NVIDIA Research and Inferact (Jian Hu et al.): REINFORCE Zero: Kernel Alignment Unlocks Stable Asynchronous RL with Importance Sampling . All numbers in sections 2 to 4 come from it. In synchronous RL, rollout and training take turns, and each waits for the other. Asynchronous RL runs them at the same time: rollout keeps generating while the learner updates. The price is weight lag . A sample generated with weights version v is trained at version k > v. The gap k − v is not small: REINFORCE Zero runs at lag 2 and 8 on math reasoning, and at lag 64 on agentic tool use. So the learner always trains on samples from an older policy. The standard correction is importance sampling (IS): reweight each token by π / μ, the learner's probability for it divided by the probability the rollout recorded when it sampled it. The question is whether that correction covers the whole gap. π is the learner's computation and μ is the rollout engine's. The second term compares the two at the same weights θv. Weight lag changes smoothly. It telescopes over the most recent updates, and when each update is small it follows a smoothly changing policy trajectory. This is the gap IS is meant to correct. Kernel mismatch fluctuates. It depends on batch composition and numerical execution, so it introduces fluctuations even when rollout and learner use identical weights. Figure 1: Peak-to-median ratio of the importance-weight deviation D3, log scale, for two asynchronous runs on DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B: REINFORCE Zero with aligned kernels and IS with standard kernels. Source: REINFORCE Zero, Table 2. The REINFORCE Zero paper measures this with D3, the per-update average of w − 1 − log w over tokens, where w is the importance weight. Each token's term is 0 when w = 1 and grows as w moves away from 1. With aligned kernels, D3 peaks at 1.50× its median: unclipped IS keeps the remaining weight-lag mismatch smooth and c

title: Release 2.74.0 corresponding to NGC container 26.10
summary:
Triton Inference Server

The Triton Inference Server provides a cloud inferencing solution optimized for both CPUs and GPUs. The server provides an inference service via an HTTP or GRPC endpoint, allowing remote clients to request inferencing for any model being managed by the server. For edge deployments, Triton Server is also available as a shared library with an API that allows the full functionality of the server to be included directly in an application.

New Features and Improvements

  • The S3 addressing style is now configurable.
  • Request cancellation is now checked before a request is dispatched to the backend, and before batch assembly in the TensorRT backend.
  • Tutorials: The Llava1.5 guide is deprecated in favor of the new Qwen2.5-VL guide for the TensorRT-LLM PyTorch backend. Note: this is a breaking change.
  • HTTP request buffers are now released after a request is rejected for exceeding the chunk limit.
  • --http-max-input-size is now enforced across nested parameters of generate requests.
  • SageMaker model URLs are now validated before path normalization.
  • Fixed copying of the cuBLAS libraries to the CUDA targets lib directory.
  • Relaxed the openai and pydantic pins to match vLLM requirements.
  • Tritonserver is now built on, and shipped on, the cuda-dl-base devel image.
  • Python backend: Restrictive permissions are now applied to shared memory, and GPU tensor allocation now falls back to host memory.
  • ONNX Runtime, OpenVINO, Python and TensorRT-LLM backends: Backend builds now require TRITON_BUILD_CONTAINER instead of synthesizing a py3-min image.
  • vLLM backend: Added support for vLLM >= 0.30, and prompts are now rendered before generation and encoding.
  • Triton CLI: The image fetch in the TRT-LLM preprocessing template is now bounded.

Known Issues

  • The Triton TensorRT-LLM Backend container image is not included in this release.
  • vLLM's v0 API and Ray are affected by vulnerabilities. Users should consider their own architecture and mitigation steps which may include but should not be limited to:
    • Do not expose Ray executors and vLLM hosts to a network where any untrusted connections might reach the host.
    • Ensure that only the other vLLM hosts are able to connect to the TCP port used for the XPUB socket. Note that the port used is random.
  • When using Valgrind or other leak detection tools on AGX-Thor or DGX-Spark systems, you might see memory leaks attributed to NvRmGpuLibOpen.
  • Valgrind or other memory leak detection tools may occasionally report leaks related to DCGM. These reports are intermittent and often disappear on retry.
  • CuPy has issues with the CUDA 13 Device API in multithreaded contexts. Avoid using tritonclient cuda_shared_memory APIs in multithreaded environments until fixed by CuPy.
  • TensorRT calibration cache may require size adjustment in some cases, which was observed for the IGX platform.
  • The core Python binding may incur an additional D2H and H2D copy if the backend and frontend both specify device memory to be used for response tensors.
  • A segmentation fault related to DCGM and NSCQ may be encountered during server shutdown on NVSwitch systems. A possible workaround for this issue is to disable the collection of GPU metrics tritonserver --allow-gpu-metrics false ....
  • When using TensorRT models, if auto-complete configuration is disabled and is_non_linear_format_io:true for reformat-free tensors is not provided in the model configuration, the model may not load successfully.
  • When using Python models in decoupled mode, users need to ensure that the ResponseSender goes out of scope or is properly cleaned up before unloading the model to guarantee that the unloading process executes correctly.
  • Triton Inference Server with vLLM backend currently does not support running vLLM models with tensor parallelism sizes greater than 1 and the default "distributed_executor_backend" setting when using explicit model control mode. In attempt to load a vllm model (tp > 1) in explicit mode, users could potentially see failure at initialize step: could not acquire lock for <_io.BufferedWriter name='<stdout>'> at interpreter shutdown, possibly due to daemon threads. For the default model control mode, after server shutdown, vllm related sub-processes are not killed. Related vllm issue: vllm-project/vllm#6766. Please specify "distributed_executor_backend":"ray" in the model.json when deploying vllm models with tensor parallelism > 1.
  • When loading models with file override, multiple model configuration files are not supported. Users must provide the model configuration by setting parameter "config" : "<JSON>" instead of custom configuration file in the following format: "file:configs/<model-config-name>.pbtxt" : "<base64-encoded-file-content>".
  • TensorRT-LLM backend provides limited support of Triton extensions and features.
  • The TensorRT-LLM backend may core dump on server shutdown. This impacts server teardown only and will not impact inferencing.
  • The Java CAPI is known to have intermittent segfaults.
  • Some systems which implement malloc() may not release memory back to the operating system right away causing a false memory leak. This can be mitigated by using a different malloc implementation. Tcmalloc and jemalloc are installed in the Triton container and can be used by specifying the library in LD_PRELOAD. NVIDIA recommends experimenting with both tcmalloc and jemalloc to determine which one works better for your use case.
  • Auto-complete may cause an increase in server start time. To avoid a start time increase, users can provide the full model configuration and launch the server with --disable-auto-complete-config.
  • Auto-complete does not support PyTorch models due to lack of metadata in the model. It can only verify that the number of inputs and the input names matches what is specified in the model configuration. There is no model metadata about the number of outputs and datatypes. Related PyTorch bug: pytorch/pytorch#38273
  • Triton Client PIP wheels for ARM SBSA are not available from PyPI and pip will install an incorrect Jetson version of Triton Client library for Arm SBSA. The correct client wheel file can be pulled directly from the Arm SBSA SDK image and manually installed.
  • Traced models in PyTorch seem to create overflows when int8 tensor values are transformed to int32 on the GPU. Refer to pytorch/pytorch#66930 for more information.
  • Triton cannot retrieve GPU metrics with MIG-enabled GPU devices.
  • Triton metrics might not work if the host machine is running a separate DCGM agent on bare-metal or in a container.

Client Libraries and Examples

The client libraries and examples are available in this release exclusively via the Ubuntu 24.04–based NGC Container. The SDK container includes the client libraries and examples, Performance Analyzer, and Model Analyzer. See Getting the Client Libraries for more information.

ManyLinux Assets (early access)

This release was compiled with AlmaLinux 8.9 based out of manylinux_2_34 and can be used on RHEL 9 and later versions.
See the included README.md for complete details about installation, verification, and support.
This release supports ensembles. Confirm CUDA, TensorRT, ONNX Runtime, PyTorch, and Python versions in the shipped README.md.
Some optional backend features such as the PyTorch backend's TorchTRT extension are not currently supported.
